stem:
Sort each complete list of thyroid disorders into the correct category.

Two categories describe structure (focal or diffuse enlargement) and two describe function (hypo- or hyperthyroidism).

items.left: Iatrogenic (oral T4 Rx) · Graves' disease · Toxic nodule/toxic MNG · Thyroiditis (painful, Hashimoto's, post-partum) · Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow)
Benign adenoma · Toxic adenoma · Papillary Ca · Follicular Ca · Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC)
Graves' · Hashimoto's · Multinodular goiter (MNG) · Iodine deficiency

answer:
The pairings:

ListCategory
Iatrogenic (oral T4 Rx) · Graves' disease · Toxic nodule/toxic MNG · Thyroiditis (painful, Hashimoto's, post-partum) · Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow)Hyperthyroidism/Thyrotoxicosis (Function)
Hashimoto's · Iatrogenic · Central (pit/hypothal) · Thyroiditis (hypo phase)Hypothyroidism (Function)
Benign adenoma · Toxic adenoma · Papillary Ca · Follicular Ca · Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC)Focal Enlargement - nodules (Structure)
Graves' · Hashimoto's · Multinodular goiter (MNG) · Iodine deficiencyDiffuse Enlargement - goitre (Structure)

Note that Graves' and Hashimoto's each appear twice, under both a Structure and a Function category - Graves' causes diffuse enlargement and hyperthyroidism; Hashimoto's causes diffuse enlargement and hypothyroidism (with a transient hyper phase). The structure/function split is the point of the exercise.
note: keyed option A + the bank's answer table

Requires hepatic and renal metabolism to form calcitriol

answer:
The pairings:

MetaboliteProperty

CholecalciferolRequires hepatic metabolism to form calcifediol
ErgocalciferolRequires hepatic and renal metabolism to form calcitriol

flags.title: The module's D2/D3 split is a convention, not chemistry
flags.html: Strictly, calcifediol and calcitriol are the D3 metabolites (25-OH-D3 and 1,25-(OH)2-D3), so both "requires hepatic metabolism to form calcifediol" and "requires hepatic and renal metabolism to form calcitriol" strictly describe cholecalciferol, and ergocalciferol (D2) actually becomes 25-OH-D2 and then 1,25-(OH)2-D2. The lecture does not separate them either: its vitamin D chart lists both ergocalciferol and cholecalciferol as needing "hepatic + renal" metabolism. The grid keeps the module's own key (cholecalciferol to calcifediol, ergocalciferol to calcitriol), so read the D2/D3 rows as the module's framing rather than a real biochemical difference.

stem: Match the type of endometrium with the phase of the menstrual cycle.
answer:
The pairings:

EndometriumMenstrual cycle phase
Secretory endometriumLuteal phase
Proliferative endometriumFollicular phase

Name each phase from the hormone driving it and the mapping cannot invert:

  • ⭐ Follicular = estrogen = PROLIFERATIVE. Oestrogen from the growing follicle thickens the endometrium, and the glands are tubular and straight
  • ⭐ Luteal = progesterone = SECRETORY. The corpus luteum primes the lining for implantation, and the glands become tortuous with luminal secretions

⭐ Under the microscope the gland shape is the tell: straight and tubular means oestrogen, coiled and secreting means progesterone. Swapping them is the classic trap.
note: keyed option A; confirmed against the Rise export (Histology and Embryology courseData: Secretory->Luteal, Proliferative->Follicular)

stem: Match each letter on the figure with the correct location in the Fallopian tube.
answer:
The pairings:

LabelLocation in the Fallopian tube
AIsthmus
BAmpulla
CInfundibulum
DFimbriae

The order is anatomical, running from the uterus outward to the ovary:

  • intramural — within the uterine wall
  • ⭐ isthmus — the thinnest, narrowest segment
  • ⭐ ampulla — the widest, most central segment, and where fertilization usually occurs
  • infundibulum — the funnel nearest the ovary
  • fimbriae — the finger-like projections at its mouth

⭐ Getting the isthmus and ampulla the right way round is the examinable half, because the ampulla being widest is the same fact that explains both normal fertilization and why 96-98% of ectopic pregnancies are tubal.
note: keyed option A; confirmed against the Rise export (Histology and Embryology, 'FT labeled.png': A-Isthmus, B-Ampulla, C-Infundibulum, D-Fimbriae). Figure recovered from articulateusercontent.com (illustration).

stem: Order the stages of ovarian follicle development from first to last.
answer:
The pairings:

StagePosition in the sequence
Oocyte1st
Primordial follicle2nd
Primary follicle3rd
Secondary follicle4th
Mature (Graafian) follicle5th

What defines each step is the granulosa and theca around the oocyte:

  • primordial — dormant, and what is present at birth. At puberty monthly ovarian factors recruit 30-50 into primary follicles
  • primary — acquires one layer of granulosa cells
  • secondary — granulosa proliferate into another layer
  • ⭐ tertiary/Graafian — a double layer of theca outside, a fluid-filled antrum, and thickened granulosa over the oocyte. It takes 6-8 months to reach this stage

⭐ The follicle with the most FSH receptors becomes dominant, because there is only so much FSH to go round — which is exactly the competition that ART defeats by flooding the system with supraphysiological FSH so several follicles mature at once.
note: keyed option A; confirmed against the Rise export (ordering 1-5)

stem: Match the correct primordial structure to the female reproductive system terminal structure.
answer:
The pairings:

Primordial structureTerminal structure
Primordial germ cellsPrimary oocytes
Cortical cordsFollicular cells
Mesonephric ductGartner's ducts
Uterovaginal primordiumUterus
Urogenital sinusLower 2/3 vagina
GubernaculumRound ligament of the uterus
Genital tubercleClitoris
Urethral foldsLabia minora
Labioscrotal swellingsLabia majora
  • Primordial Germ Cells differentiate into oogonia, which undergo active mitosis to form primary oocytes
  • Cortical cords proliferate and surround the primary oocytes differentiating into follicular cells
  • The mesonephric duct regresses during female development, but some remnants remain including Gartner's ducts lateral to the vagina
  • The uterovaginal primordium formed by fused paramesonephric ducts forms the uterus and upper 1/3 of the vagina
  • Urogenital Sinus forms sinovaginal bulbs with the uterovaginal primordium to form the vagina - the urogenital sinus forms the lower 2/3 of the vagina and the uterovaginal primordium forms the upper 1/3
  • The gubernaculum attaches to the uterus forming the ligament of the ovary cranially and the round ligament of the uterus caudally
  • The genital tubercle elongates to form the clitoris
  • The urethral folds stay separate to form the labia minora
  • The labioscrotal swelling expand to form the labia majora
note: keyed option C + answer table; confirmed against the Rise export (Development of the Female Reproductive Tract). Old answer had the explanation jammed into an extra table cell; re-laid as a list.

stem: Match the correct function to the labelled structures. Each function pairs with one label A–G on the diagram.
answer:
The pairings:

FunctionLabel
Hormone producerE - Ovary
Childbirth passageC - Vagina
Carries ovarian vesselsG - Suspensory ligament of the ovary
Home to developing fetusA - Body of the uterus
Common site of fertilizationD - Ampulla of the uterine tube
Anchors ovary to uterusF - Ligament of the ovary
Site of Pap smearsB - Cervix

The reasoning below is mine — the module keyed the letters and gave none.

  • F and G are the pair worth separating. The ligament of the ovary (F) runs medially from the ovary to the uterus and is a gubernaculum remnant carrying nothing. The suspensory ligament (G) runs laterally over the pelvic brim and is the one holding the ovarian artery, vein and nerves — which is why it is the pedicle clamped in an oophorectomy, and why the ureter running beneath it is what gets injured.
  • D is the uterine tube, and fertilization happens in its ampulla, the widest part; the fimbriae at its lateral end only sweep the oocyte in. A tubal ectopic implants here for the same reason.
  • B is the cervix because a Pap samples the transformation zone, where columnar endocervical epithelium meets squamous ectocervical epithelium. That junction is where HPV transforms cells — not the uterine body (A), and not the vagina (C).
note: keyed option C + answer table; confirmed against the Rise export ('KC Reproductive Organs.png')

stem: Match the correct marker substance for each pathology.
answer:
The pairings:

PathologyMarker
DysgerminomaLDH
Yolk sac tumora-FP
Choriocarcinomab-hCG

Each germ cell tumour is named by the tissue it is trying to be, and the marker follows from that. The lecture's marker table sets out three strong associations:

  • Dysgerminoma → LDH. The ovarian counterpart of the seminoma; LDH is its marker.
  • Yolk sac tumour → alpha-fetoprotein. AFP is what a yolk sac makes, so a tumour differentiating towards yolk sac makes it too. Most common in toddlers, and Schiller-Duval bodies on histology are pathognomonic.
  • Choriocarcinoma → beta-hCG. It arises from placental tissue, and beta-hCG is the placental hormone.

Worth holding onto: immature teratoma and embryonal carcinoma each raise two of the three weakly, which is why the table marks the three above as the strong, discriminating associations rather than the only ones.
